metaLine: 108 BPM · 4/4 · one of the brisk Friday night zemirot · five stanzas of four lines, and each stanza rhymes on a single sound
intro: One of the standard Friday night zemirot, and the one that argues rather than praises. Its claim is that the Sabbath is evidence — that the people who keep it and remember it are witnesses to how the world was made, and that the day itself is the testimony. Five stanzas, each rhyming on one sound throughout, and the acrostic of the first letters spells a name that is no longer certain.

stanzas.label: the witnesses

lines.en: Rest and joy, a light for the Jews;
a day of Sabbath rest, a day of delights.
Those who keep it and those who remember it, they are the witnesses
that in six days all things were created, and they stand.

stanzas.summary: {{2.0}} and {{2.1}} are the two verbs of the two versions of the fourth commandment — keep it, in Deuteronomy, and remember it, in Exodus. The poem does not choose between them either; it makes the people who do both into witnesses, which is a legal word, and {{2.3}} is the legal term for testimony.

stanzas.label: everything made

lines.en: The highest heavens, earth and seas,
all the host on high, lofty and exalted,
sea creature and man and the wild ox,
for the LORD is God, the Rock of worlds.

stanzas.summary: The inventory runs from the top of the sky to the animals, and the last line names the maker. {{7.1}} is a short form of the divine name, the one that appears at the end of halleluyah, and putting it next to the full name in {{7.2}} is deliberate.

stanzas.label: keep it holy

lines.en: He it is who spoke to the treasured people:
keep it, to make it holy, from its coming in to its going out.
The holy Sabbath, the day of His delight,
for on it God rested from all His work.

stanzas.summary: {{9.2}} and {{9.4}} mark the boundaries of the day by sunset rather than by clock — its coming in and its going out — which is still the ordinary Hebrew for when Shabbat starts and ends. This is the practical stanza: the previous two argue, this one instructs.

stanzas.label: he will strengthen you

lines.en: By the commandment of the Sabbath God will strengthen you;
rise, call out to Him, He will hurry to make you strong.
The soul of every living thing, and also we will revere You.
Eat in joy, for He has already accepted you.

stanzas.summary: {{15.0}} is an imperative — eat — and the reason given is that the acceptance has already happened. The poem is being sung at a table with food on it, and this is the line that gives permission to enjoy it, which is the ordinary theology of the Sabbath meal stated in five words.

stanzas.label: two loaves

lines.en: With a double portion of bread and the great kiddush,
with abundance of delicacies and a generous spirit,
those who take delight in it will merit great good,
at the coming of the redeemer, for the life of the world to come.

stanzas.summary: {{16.0}} is the two loaves on the table, named as the poem is being sung over them. It closes on {{19.3}} and {{19.4}} — the world to come — so the last stanza runs from the bread in front of you to the end of history in four lines.

chantTips: Brisk. Around 108 BPM, faster than Tzur Mishelo, and it works well early in the meal while people still have energy.
Every line of a stanza rhymes with every other. If a line does not land on that sound, you have skipped one.
There is no refrain, which is what makes this one harder for guests than Tzur Mishelo — a table that does not know it will not join in halfway.
The last line of each stanza is where the melody resolves. Let it sit before starting the next.

about.body: The song's claim is unusual for a table song: that Sabbath observance is evidence for creation, and that the observers are witnesses in the legal sense. It states the claim in the first stanza, produces the inventory of what was made in the second, and only then gets to the practicalities.
Exodus says remember the Sabbath day; Deuteronomy says keep it. The difference has been discussed for two thousand years, and this poem simply uses both in one line and moves on.

The acrostic spells a name, and which Moshe it refers to is not settled. Unlike Dror Yikra, whose author signed it and is known, this one carries a signature that no longer identifies anybody with certainty.
